## R Markdown

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document. You can embed an R code chunk like this:

```{r cars}
summary(cars)
```

## Including Plots

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(pressure)
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

m<-matrix(data=c(1,2,3,4,5,6),nrow=2,ncol=3,byrow=TRUE)
this will align the matrix to count from left to right, aka by row
m<-matrix(data=c(1,2,3,4,5,6),nrow=2,ncol=3,byrow=FALSE)
this will align the matrix to count from top to bottom, aka by column

v1<-c(1,2,3,4)
v2<-c(6,7,8,9)
m1<-rbind(v1,v2)
this will bind the vectors on top of each other in two rows

m2<-cbind(v1,v2)
this will bind the vectors next to eachother in two columns

dim(m1) will tell you the number of rows (at 1) and the number of columns at index position 2

str(m2) will tell details about a project

array(data=1:90),dim=c(5,6,3) will create an array with 5 rows, 6 columns, and 3 levels

after assigning a matrix, you can extract specific rows and columns and attach to a variable "x" using x<-m[row,column]... to do a group of multiple rows and columns, prefix the row/column numbers with c()

to replace an elemnt of a matrix, identify the row and column number with m[row,column] and assign the new level as you would any other variable, with <- followed by the new value (note: to do a whole column/row, leave the unchanged spot blank, e.g.: m[,8]<-2 will change all of column 8 to 2)

after making a list, to extract a single component of the list, use l[[x]], where x=the number from the list you want to extract
if that element is a matrix and you want it to be a specific row and column in that matrix, follow the command with [row,column] of your choosing

l[1:2] will extract the first two components of that list. To do specific numbers, use l[c(x,y)], where x and y are the numbers on the list you want to extract (e.g., l[c(1,3)] will give you the first and third elements on the list)

names(l)<-c("name1", "name2",...) will name the items on the list
data.frame() will make a list of titles and values based on how you frame it. E.g.: df <- data.frame (first heading = c("value1", "value2",...), second heading = c("value1", "value2",...), etc.)

df<-read.csv("~/Desktop/randompeople-module4.csv",sep=",",header=TRUE, stringsAsFactors=FALSE) assigns a data frame to a csv file. sep= will separate the header names, header=true denotes that the first line is names of the columns, stringsAsFactors= will determine how R handles the columns... true will be best for statistical models (e.g. if a title is treatment, with values of frozen,raw,cooked, R will be able to compare those values against eachother and/or rank. =false will treat the columns as individual text with individual values (e.g. if a title is dob, each value is unique to that row)

df<-cbind(df,id=c(x,y,...)) will add additional columns/variables to a data frame. rbind will add additional rows/cases
OR, you can use "$" to add a new variable (e.g. df$school<-c(list of schools)), but this will add "school" as a character vector rather than a factor

a character vector stores raw text strings, where a factor stores categorical data using an underlying structure of integers mapped to predefined text labels called levels (i.e. a character vector is an open-ended notepad, and a dactor is a multiple choice dropdown menu)

new_df<- df[df$columnname == value,] will create a subset under the conditions you set for which column and which value you want to extract

new_df<-df[df$columnname == value, c("column1", "column2", "column3"...)] will create a subset under the conditions you've set with only the columns that you select to include

na.rm=TRUE will remove NAs (missing data) from a calculation

Inf (and-Inf) is a numerical calculation too extreme to express

NaN will be a result if a calculation is not a number, like a square root of a negative number

a plain text file can be read using read.table(), where file= is the argument and header=true/false depending on field names; the sep=argument tells R what character is used as a separator or deliminater in the file; the skip= argument can be used to start reading a file after a set number of rows

head(d) = first 6 lines of data (request more by [n:n] at end)
tail(d) = last 6 lines of data
for .txt files, sep= or delim = is "\t"
for.csv files, sep= or delim= is ","

d<-read_csv(file vector,header=TRUE,sep=,stringsAsFactors=FALSE) 
for loading a data file

str() tells you the info about a data set (numrows,numcolums) where head() previews the set so you can confirm you're reading the right data
dim() returns the number of rows and columns in a dataframe
also remember names(), colnames(), rownames()

attach() binds the variables from the data fram named as an argument to the local namespace so that as long as the data frame is attached, variables can be caller by their names without explicitly referring to the datafram (don't need to use $ or bracket notation)
-> remember to detach() when finished

summary() gives a quick overview of wach column in a data frame
--> numeric values will show a minimum, 25th percentile, median, mean, 75th percentile, and maximum
--> factors will receive a count

to use median(), remember that calling to the column name requires d$ as a prefix in order for R to know where you are referring to

you can create a new variable that is a function of other column information
--> for example: population density = population/area
-->d$density<-d$population/d$area

to get the n number of highest values, use order()
--> d<-d[order(-d$value),] followed by d[1:10,]
to get the n number of lowest values, use order()
--> d<-d[order(d$value),] followed by d[1:10,]

to extract a new variable containing a certain group of information from your dataset, use grep() or order()
--> to get information on the top 20 largest values from a column, use new<-d[order(d$column),] followed by new[1:20,]
you can then get information on these top 20 by assigning new[1:20,] to a new vector (x)
to do subsequent calculations (e.g. median), use median (x$column,na.rm=TRUE)
--> to do it based on the first letter of the name, use grep()
--> e.g. to get data from countries beginning with A through F, use new<-d[grep("^[A-F]",d$country),]

par(mfrow=c(r,c)) will set up a panel of n number of row (r) and columns(c)
this can be useful when making a panel of box plots and bar plots, for example. follow this commmant with a list of boxplot(d$column) and barplot(d$column) that you want to include

hist(log(d$column),freq=FALSE,col="red",main="Title",xlab="xaxislabel",ylab="yaxislabel",ylim=c(yaxisscale))


in hist(), setting freq=FALSE will scale the Y acis to represent the proportion of observations falling into each bin rather than the count

to add a line of a mean value to your histogram, use abline(v=mean((d$column),na.rm=TRUE),col="",lwd=#,lty="dashed")
--> v= vertical, h=horizontal
-->lwd=line width/thickness
-->lty= line type (dashed,dotted, 2)

to superimpose a density() curve onto a histogram, use lines(density()) function
--> lines(density(d$value),col="")

sort() can be used to sort a dataset into a table when combined with table()
-->e.g.: to find the most common form of a variable, use sort(table(d$column),decreasing=TRUE)
-->note: to find the least common, use decreasing=FALSE

~ can be used as "by", so if you want to make a box plot of a variable on y by x, you would use "boxplot(d$columny)~d$columnx) 

p <- ggplot(data = d, aes(x = column, y = column))  #define the variables
p <- p + geom_boxplot()  #graph them in a boxplot
p <- p + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90))  #put x-axis names at 90deg
p <- p + ylab("yaxislabel")  #rename y-axis title
p  #show me the graph

scatterplot: use plot(x=$column, y=d$column)

p <- ggplot(data = d, aes(x = column, y = column), color = factor(column)))  # first, we build a plot object and color points by a specific variable
p <- p + xlab("xaxislabel") + ylab("yaxislabel")  # then we modify the axis labels
p <- p + geom_point()  # then we make a scatterplot
p <- p + theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank())  # then we modify the legend to haave no legend title
p  # and, finally, we plot the object

if you wanted the above variables to be separated in a grid, use facet_wrap()
p<-p+facet_wrap(~column,ncol=4) #the column is the same used in factor(column) above
p<-p+theme(legend.position="none")
p

to add a linear regression line: p + geom_smooth(method="lm", full range=TRUE)
--> lm = linear model (straight ordinary least squares)
-->loess=local regression (localized polynomial curves)
-->gam=generalized additive model (smooth splines, scalabale alternative to loess for larger datasets)
-->glm=generalized linear model (for non-continuous outcomes (logistic regression for binary data))

you can change the formula of the shape of the line to not be y~x by including ,formula = in the argument above
--> quadratic: formula = y~poly(x,2)
-->logarithmic: formula=y~log(x)
--> se: standard error confidence band (TRUE displays the grey shadow)
--> level: defaults to 95% confidence
--> span=controls how wiggly the curve is, defaults to 0.75

include p<-p+geom_point() priot to the geom_smooth() argument to include scatter points underneath the line

aggregate() gives a summary of statistics defined by a particular function FUN=
e.g. aggregate(d$column1 ~ d$column1, FUN="mean", na.rm=TRUE) will give the mean of the column1 values sorted by column2

reminder, d["column']=d$column

use %>% to pipe together a long line of code
e.g.: to add a variable "binomial" to a data fram concatenating Genus and Species, trimming the data to only include binomial, family, mean female body mass and mean male body mass, grouped by binomial and averages calculated:
s <- d %>%
+ mutate(Binomial = paste(Genus, Species, sep = " ")) %>%
+ select(Binomial, Body_mass_female_mean, Body_mass_male_mean) %>%
+ group_by(Binomial) %>%
+ summarise(avgF = mean(Body_mass_female_mean, na.rm = TRUE), avgM = mean(Body_mass_male_mean,na.rm = TRUE), na.rm = TRUE))
> s
